title: Midterm
subtitle: Forces, Kinematics, Projectiles, Kinetics, Work & Energy

items.text: Define force, and tell internal forces from external ones
Explain mass vs. weight, and get weight (with its sign) from mass
Tell static, dynamic, and rolling friction apart
Use F = μN to solve for friction OR the normal force
Convert lb to N and lb to kg with the equation sheet
Combine several forces into a resultant (magnitude and direction)
Break a force into vertical and horizontal components with sin and cos
Set up a runner's external forces correctly, including body weight
Solve a static equilibrium problem for an unknown force or mass
Find the resultant force and acceleration of a skier on a slope
Define kinematics and name the four types of motion with examples
Find distance, displacement, and yards gained
Explain speed vs. velocity, and calculate both
Calculate acceleration as (final - initial) / time with the right sign
Explain why constant speed around a curve is still acceleration
Know what the slopes of position-time and velocity-time graphs give
Use d = vᵢt + ½at² and convert mph to m/s
Define a projectile and explain why horizontal and vertical are independent
Know the vertical acceleration at takeoff, at the peak, and through flight
Split a release velocity into vₓ and vᵧ (and combine them back)
Explain how velocity, angle, and height affect distance
Calculate max height (and remember to add the starting height)
Pick the right flight time equation and calculate flight time
Calculate horizontal displacement
State Newton's three laws and match each to an example
Use F = ma with the NET force to find acceleration
Calculate momentum with units converted to kg and m/s
Use impulse-momentum, subtracting weight for vertical problems
Explain why mats and follow-through change force or momentum
Explain when momentum is conserved and solve a simple collision
Calculate the coefficient of restitution and explain what affects it
Calculate work and tell whether it's positive or negative
Connect positive/negative work to concentric/eccentric muscle action
Calculate KE, GPE, strain energy, and total mechanical energy
Use work = change in energy to find a force or a height
Explain when mechanical energy is conserved
Calculate power from work and time (or force and velocity)

blocks.p: A **force** is a push or a pull, and the big idea is that it's the thing that can **accelerate** an object. No force, no change in motion. We measure it in Newtons (N) or pounds (lb), and the conversion you'll use most is **1 lb = 4.45 N** (it's on your equation sheet).

**Internal forces** act inside the body or system you're looking at, like muscles pulling on tendons or forces on your ligaments and bones. **External forces** come from the body interacting with its surroundings: gravity, air resistance, friction, the ground pushing back. When this class asks for a resultant, it almost always means the resultant of the **external** forces.

blocks.h: Mass vs. weight (they are not the same thing)

blocks.p: **Mass** is how much inertia something has, meaning how hard it is to change its motion. It's measured in kg and it **never changes**, Earth, Moon, or deep space. **Weight** is the downward pull from gravity on that mass, so it depends on where you are. On Earth, `W = mg` with g = -9.8 m/s/s, and weight comes out **negative** because it points down.

Forget the everyday meaning of "normal." Here, **normal force** is the force **perpendicular to the surface**: the ground pushing up on your foot, or your hand squeezing a racket grip. Friction always depends on it: `F = μN`, where μ is the coefficient of friction (it has no units).

head: Type
When it happens
Example
rows: Two dry surfaces NOT moving relative to each other
A running shoe planted on the track
Two dry surfaces sliding across each other
A skater gliding, a shuffleboard puck
A rolling object deforming against a surface

blocks.p: One subtle thing: for **static** friction, `F = μN` gives the **maximum** friction you can get before slipping starts. For dynamic friction it gives the actual friction. The static coefficient is usually a bit bigger than the dynamic one, which is why it's harder to get something sliding than to keep it sliding.

blocks.key: Weight = mass x -9.8, and it's negative. Mass never changes. Friction = μ x normal force, and on flat ground with no vertical acceleration the normal force is just the size of body weight.

example.q: An astronaut has a mass of 84 kg. What is his weight on Earth, and what is his weight floating in deep space?
example.a: Earth: 84 x -9.8 = **-823 N**. Deep space: no gravity, so **0 N**. His mass is still 84 kg in both places.

example.q: A 50 kg skater glides with a dynamic friction coefficient of 0.08. What's the friction force?
example.a: Normal force = 50 x 9.8 = 490 N. Friction = 0.08 x 490 = **39 N**. Common mistake: multiplying μ by the mass (50) instead of the normal force.

example.q: Tammy's hand-racket coefficient is 0.57 and she needs 120 N of friction along the racket. How hard does she squeeze?
example.a: Here friction is known and N is the unknown: 120 = 0.57 x N, so N = 120 / 0.57 = **211 N**.

blocks.p: The **resultant** (or net) force is what you get when you add up every external force on something. Forces are **vectors**, so they have a size (magnitude) AND a direction, which means you can't just add the numbers. You build a right triangle.

blocks.h: Sine, cosine, tangent are just ratios

blocks.p: Your trig functions are ratios of sides of a right triangle. Cosine of an angle tells you how long the adjacent side is compared to the hypotenuse. Sine does the opposite side. Tangent is opposite over adjacent. So if the angle is measured **from horizontal**, the vertical piece is the opposite side (use **sine**) and the horizontal piece is the adjacent side (use **cosine**). Inverse tangent goes backwards: give it opposite/adjacent and it hands you the angle.

steps: Draw it. Pick which way is positive for horizontal and vertical, and stay consistent.
Combine all the **parallel** forces first. Same direction, add. Opposite directions, subtract. You should end up with ONE horizontal number and ONE vertical number.
Put them **tip to tail**: start anywhere, draw the first arrow, and start the second arrow where the first one's arrowhead ends. That's what keeps the triangle from getting flipped.
Magnitude: Pythagorean theorem, `c = √(a² + b²)`.
Direction: `θ = tan⁻¹(opposite / adjacent)`. "Relative to horizontal" or "relative to the ground" means horizontal is 0°. "Relative to vertical" means use the other angle (90° minus it).

blocks.tip: On "external force" problems, flip the athlete's push into the ground's reaction. If a runner pushes forward into the ground at foot strike, the ground pushes **back** on the runner (Newton's third law). That backward push is what goes in your diagram. And don't forget body weight is pulling down the whole time.

blocks.p: This is the same triangle run in reverse. You know the hypotenuse and the angle, and you want the two legs: vertical = R x sin(θ), horizontal = R x cos(θ), when θ is from horizontal.

When all the external forces add up to zero, the object is in **equilibrium**, and that means it isn't **accelerating**. It does NOT mean it isn't moving. A puck gliding at constant speed is in equilibrium too. For a static equilibrium problem, set the up forces equal to the down forces and solve for the unknown.

blocks.key: Combine parallel forces first, then Pythagoras for size and inverse tangent for angle. Sine gets the side opposite your angle, cosine gets the side next to it. Read "relative to horizontal vs. vertical" carefully.

example.q: A 68 kg runner pushes 180 N forward into the ground at foot strike. Vertical ground reaction force is 1250 N, and 105 N of air resistance works against him. Find the resultant external force and its direction relative to the ground.
example.a: Horizontal: the ground pushes back 180 N, plus 105 N of air, so 285 N backward. Vertical: 1250 up minus his weight (68 x 9.8 = 666 N down) = 584 N up. Magnitude = √(285² + 584²) = **650 N**. Angle = tan⁻¹(584 / 285) = **64°** from horizontal, pointing up and back. The classic mistake is leaving out body weight, which gives you about 77° instead.

example.q: A long jumper's ground reaction force is 6700 N at 67° from horizontal. Find the vertical and horizontal components.
example.a: Vertical = 6700 x sin 67° = **6167 N**. Horizontal = 6700 x cos 67° = **2618 N**.

example.q: A cheerleader (170 lb) holds a partner up in a handstand. The vertical ground reaction force is 1355 N. What's the partner's mass if everything is in equilibrium?
example.a: Get everything in Newtons: 170 x 4.45 = 756.5 N. The ground holds up both people, so the partner's weight is 1355 - 756.5 = 598.5 N. Mass = 598.5 / 9.8 = **61 kg**.

blocks.p: On a slope, gravity still pulls straight down, but that straight-down weight gets split into two pieces: one that **pulls you down the slope** and one that **presses you into the slope**. The pressing piece is the normal force, which is what friction depends on.

head: Piece of weight
Formula
What it does
rows: Sets how much friction you get

blocks.p: The angle of the slope shows up again inside the little force triangle, because the two triangles are similar (they both have a right angle and they share a corner). That's why the slope angle goes right into sine and cosine. If drawing it trips you up, you can just trust the formula. It's on your equation sheet as `F_Slope = -mg sin θ` (the negative there just means g is negative, so the result comes out positive).

steps: Weight: m x 9.8.
Downhill pull: weight x sin(slope angle).
If friction isn't given, find it: normal force = weight x cos(angle), then friction = μ x normal.
Resultant along the slope = downhill pull minus friction minus air resistance. Air resistance points against the direction of motion, so on a slope it points back up the slope.
If they ask for acceleration: a = resultant / mass.

blocks.key: Down the slope uses sine, into the slope (normal) uses cosine. Subtract friction and air from the downhill pull, then divide by mass if they want acceleration. Expect one of these on the midterm with an acceleration step added.

example.q: A 67 kg skier glides down an 18° slope with 91 N of friction and 68 N of air resistance. Find the resultant force and the acceleration.
example.a: Weight = 67 x 9.8 = 657 N. Downhill pull = 657 x sin 18° = 203 N. Resultant = 203 - 91 - 68 = **44 N** in the direction of motion. Acceleration = 44 / 67 = **0.66 m/s/s**.

example.q: A 60 kg skier is moving down a 30° slope. Air resistance is 10 N and the dynamic friction coefficient is 0.08. What's the resultant force?
example.a: Weight = 588 N. Normal = 588 x cos 30° = 509 N, so friction = 0.08 x 509 = 41 N. Downhill pull = 588 x sin 30° = 294 N. Resultant = 294 - 41 - 10 = **243 N** down the slope.

questions.question: Which of these best defines a force?
options: A push or pull that can accelerate an object
The amount of matter an object contains
The rate at which an object changes position
The resistance an object has to moving
questions.explanation: A force is a push or pull, and its defining ability is to accelerate an object. Mass is the amount of matter (and inertia).

questions.question: Which of these is an internal force?
options: Gravity pulling down on the body
The muscle force pulling on a tendon
questions.explanation: Internal forces act inside the system being studied. Gravity, air resistance, and friction all come from the body's surroundings, so they're external.

questions.question: A cyclist is riding down the road. Which of these are EXTERNAL forces on the cyclist and bike? (Select all that apply)
options: The ground pushing up on the bike
questions.explanation: External = from the surroundings: rolling friction, air resistance, gravity (weight), and the ground's reaction. Muscle and ligament forces are internal.

questions.question: An astronaut's mass is 84 kg. What is his weight on Earth? (g = -9.8 m/s/s)
questions.explanation: W = mg = 84 x -9.8 = -823 N. Weight points down, so it's negative. 84 kg is his mass, not his weight.

questions.question: That same 84 kg astronaut is now floating in deep space with no gravity. Which statement is true?
options: His mass is 0 kg and his weight is 0 N
His mass is 84 kg and his weight is -823 N
His mass is 0 kg and his weight is -823 N
His mass is 84 kg and his weight is 0 N
questions.explanation: Mass never changes with location. Weight depends on gravity, so with no gravity it's zero.

questions.question: A sprinter's shoe is planted on the track during the stance phase and is not sliding. What kind of friction is acting?
questions.explanation: Static friction acts between two surfaces that are not moving relative to each other. Dynamic friction is for sliding surfaces.

questions.question: For STATIC friction, what does F = μN actually tell you?
options: The exact friction acting at every moment of contact
The most friction possible before the surfaces start to slip
The friction acting once the surfaces start sliding
The smallest friction needed to start any motion at all
questions.explanation: For static friction, μN is the maximum before slipping. Below that, static friction only matches whatever force is trying to slide the surfaces.

questions.question: Which unit conversion is on your equation sheet and correct?
questions.explanation: 1 lb = 4.45 N (and 1 kg = 2.2 lb). To go from pounds to Newtons, multiply by 4.45.

questions.question: A 50 kg ice skater glides across the ice. The coefficient of dynamic friction is 0.06. What's the friction force?
questions.explanation: Normal force = 50 x 9.8 = 490 N. Friction = 0.06 x 490 = 29.4 N. Using 50 instead of 490 is the classic slip.

questions.question: The static friction coefficient between Tammy's hand and racket is 0.71. What's the minimum squeeze (normal force) to exert 154 N along the racket's long axis?
questions.explanation: 154 = 0.71 x N, so N = 154 / 0.71 = 217 N. Here friction is given and normal force is the unknown.

questions.question: Which of these are VECTOR quantities (they have both size and direction)? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Force, displacement, velocity, and acceleration all have direction. Speed and mass only have size, so they're scalars.

questions.question: A sprinter pushes back on the block with 605 N (horizontal) and down with 740 N (vertical). What's the magnitude of the resultant?
questions.explanation: Perpendicular forces: √(605² + 740²) = 956 N. You can't just add vectors at right angles.

questions.question: Same sprinter (605 N back, 740 N down). What's the direction of the resultant force the sprinter applies, relative to the ground?
questions.explanation: tan θ = 740 / 605, θ = 50.7°. Relative to the ground means horizontal is 0°, and the push is down and back, so it's below horizontal. 39.3° would be relative to vertical.

questions.question: A long jumper's ground reaction force is 7340 N, forward and upward at 71° from horizontal. What's the VERTICAL component?
questions.explanation: The vertical side is opposite the 71° angle, so use sine: 7340 x sin 71° = 6940 N.

questions.question: A ground reaction force of 6700 N acts at 67° from horizontal. What's the HORIZONTAL component?
questions.explanation: The horizontal side is adjacent to the angle, so use cosine: 6700 x cos 67° = 2618 N.

questions.question: A 68 kg runner pushes 195 N forward into the ground as she contacts it. The vertical ground reaction force is 1370 N, and 100 N of air resistance acts against her. What's the direction of the resultant EXTERNAL force relative to the ground?
questions.explanation: Horizontal: ground pushes back 195 N + 100 N air = 295 N back. Vertical: 1370 - 666 (her weight) = 704 N up. tan⁻¹(704/295) = 67°. Forgetting weight gives 78°; forgetting air gives 75°.

questions.question: The resultant of all external forces on an object is zero. What must be true?
options: It must be standing completely still
It is moving with a slowly rising speed
It is not accelerating, though it could be moving
It must be moving at a constant speed
questions.explanation: Zero resultant = equilibrium = no acceleration. It can be still or moving at a constant velocity, like a gliding puck.

questions.question: A cheerleader does a handstand on another cheerleader's hands. The bottom cheerleader weighs 167 lb and the vertical ground reaction force is 1277 N. What must the top cheerleader's mass be for equilibrium?
questions.explanation: 167 lb x 4.45 = 743.1 N. The ground supports both: 1277 - 743.1 = 533.9 N for the top person. Mass = 533.9 / 9.8 = 54.5 kg.

questions.question: A 65 kg skier glides down a 20° slope. What's the NORMAL force between the skis and the snow?
questions.explanation: Normal force is the part of weight pressing into the slope: 637 x cos 20° = 599 N. The 218 N answer is the downhill pull (sine).

questions.question: A 60 kg skier glides down a 27° slope with 82 N of friction and 155 N of air resistance. What's the resultant force on the skier?
options: 267 N in the direction of motion
30 N in the direction of motion
287 N in the direction of motion
504 N in the direction of motion
questions.explanation: Downhill pull = 588 x sin 27° = 267 N. Friction and air both point back up the slope: 267 - 82 - 155 = 30 N.

questions.question: A 67 kg skier glides down an 18° slope with 91 N of friction and 68 N of air resistance. What's the skier's acceleration down the slope?
questions.explanation: Resultant = 203 - 91 - 68 = 43.9 N. a = F/m = 43.9 / 67 = 0.66 m/s/s. Divide by mass, not weight.

lessons.title: Types of motion, distance vs. displacement

blocks.p: **Kinematics** is just *describing* motion: where something is, how fast it's going, how that's changing. It doesn't care what caused it. (The *causes*, meaning forces, are **kinetics**, which is Chapter 4.)
To fully describe where something is in space you need **six** numbers: three for location (x, y, z) and three for orientation (rotation around each of those axes).

head: Type
What's happening
Example
rows: A sled sliding straight down a hill with the rider frozen in place
A skier going over a jump without tilting or spinning
Every point rotates around an axis
Your forearm rotating at the elbow during a curl
A mix of at least two of the above
Running or cycling: the body moves forward while the limbs rotate

blocks.p: **Distance** is how far you actually traveled along whatever path you took. **Displacement** is the straight line from where you started to where you ended, and it has a direction, so it's a vector. A marathon is always 26.2 miles of distance no matter what the displacement is. Run a full lap on a track and your displacement is zero.

Football problems add a third thing: **yards gained**, which is just the downfield **component** of the displacement. If the displacement line makes an angle with the sideline, yards gained = displacement x cos(that angle), since the sideline runs downfield.

blocks.key: Distance = actual path, displacement = straight line from start to finish, yards gained = displacement x cos(angle to sideline). Yards gained is always the smallest of the three.

example.q: Sam runs 55 yd before he's tackled. The straight line from start to tackle is 40 yd at 25° to the sideline. Distance, displacement, and yards gained?
example.a: Distance = **55 yd**. Displacement = **40 yd**. Yards gained = 40 x cos 25° = **36 yd**.

blocks.p: **Speed** = distance / time. **Velocity** = displacement / time. So speed is the scalar version and velocity is the vector version with a direction attached. For a marathon, speed is the useful one. For a shot put, velocity is what you need, because the direction it leaves the hand decides where it lands.

**Acceleration** = change in velocity / change in time, `a = Δv / Δt`. And any "change in" anything is **final minus initial**, always. If the final is smaller than the initial, you get a negative acceleration (slowing down in the positive direction).

Here's the concept he likes: since acceleration is based on **velocity**, and velocity includes direction, you're accelerating any time your **direction** changes, even at a constant speed. A car rounding a curve at a steady 35 mph is accelerating, and that acceleration points toward the center of the curve.
With a starting velocity and a **constant** acceleration, `d = vᵢt + ½at²`. And the velocity after that time is just `v = vᵢ + at` (that's the acceleration equation rearranged).

To turn mph into m/s, multiply by 1609 m/mile and divide by 3600 s/hour, setting it up so the units cancel. And for running, **speed = stride length x stride rate**. Increasing both always makes you faster. Increase one while cutting the other and it depends on which changes more.

blocks.tip: From the stride lab: as you speed up, stride length does most of the work at slower speeds and stride rate takes over at faster speeds. That matches the general research, but the lab video is where the exact wording came from, so defer to it if a question gets picky.

blocks.key: Speed uses distance, velocity uses displacement. Acceleration = (final - initial) / time. Constant speed around a curve is still acceleration.

example.q: A sprinter goes from 0 to 10.45 m/s in 3.72 s. What's the acceleration?
example.a: (10.45 - 0) / 3.72 = **2.81 m/s/s**. Final minus initial, so it's positive.

example.q: Ty pitches at 101 mph and the plate is 17.5 m away. How long does the batter have?
A skeleton racer enters the sled at 5.3 m/s and accelerates at 1 m/s/s. What's the displacement after 3 s?
example.a: d = 5.3(3) + ½(1)(3²) = 15.9 + 4.5 = **20.4 m**. (Velocity at that point would be 5.3 + 3 = 8.3 m/s.)

questions.question: Which branch of mechanics is concerned with DESCRIBING motion, without looking at what caused it?
questions.explanation: Kinematics describes motion (position, velocity, acceleration). Kinetics looks at the forces that cause it.

questions.question: How many values do you need to completely describe an object's position and orientation in space?
options: Six: three for location and three for orientation
Three: one for each location axis x, y, and z
Two: one horizontal and one vertical location
Four: three for location and one for its rotation
questions.explanation: Full position needs x, y, z location plus rotation about all three axes.

questions.question: A sled slides straight down a hill and the rider holds perfectly still on it. What type of motion is the rider's body doing?
questions.explanation: Straight-line path with no change in orientation is rectilinear translation.

questions.question: A cyclist rides down the road. Her body moves forward while her legs rotate around the hips and knees. What type of motion is this overall?
questions.explanation: General motion is a combination of at least two types. Here it's translation of the body plus rotation of the limbs.

questions.question: A ski jumper flies through the air along a curved path, keeping the exact same body orientation the whole time. What type of motion is this?
questions.explanation: A curved path with no change in orientation is curvilinear translation.

questions.question: Jonathan runs the football 42 yd before he's tackled. The straight line from start to tackle is 37 yd at 25° to the right sideline. How many yards did he gain?
questions.explanation: Yards gained is the downfield component of displacement: 37 x cos 25° = 33.5 yd. The sine answer is the cross-field part.

questions.question: Sam runs the football 55 yd before he's tackled. The straight line from start to tackle is 40 yd at 25° to the sideline. Distance, displacement, and yards gained?
questions.explanation: Distance = the actual path (55). Displacement = the straight line (40). Yards gained = 40 x cos 25° = 36 yd.

questions.question: What's the key difference between speed and velocity?
options: Speed uses displacement, velocity uses distance and has no direction
Speed is measured in m/s, velocity is measured in m/s/s instead
Speed uses distance, velocity uses displacement and has a direction
They are identical, velocity is only the term used for projectiles
questions.explanation: Speed = distance / time (scalar). Velocity = displacement / time (vector).

questions.question: Women's world records: 60 m in 6.92 s, 100 m in 10.49 s, 200 m in 21.34 s, 400 m in 47.60 s. Which race was run at the FASTEST average speed?
questions.explanation: Speeds: 60 m = 8.67, 100 m = 9.53, 200 m = 9.37, 400 m = 8.40 m/s. The 60 m is too short to reach top speed, and longer races can't hold it.

questions.question: A runner speeds up to pass someone, going from 3.2 m/s to 6.7 m/s in 1.07 s. What's his acceleration?
questions.explanation: a = (final - initial) / time = (6.7 - 3.2) / 1.07 = 3.27 m/s/s.

questions.question: A car drives around a curve at a constant 35 mph. Is it accelerating?
options: No, because its speed is staying the same the whole time
Yes, because its direction (and so its velocity) is changing
No, because acceleration only happens on a straight line
Yes, but only if the car is also speeding up a little
questions.explanation: Acceleration is a change in velocity, and velocity includes direction. Changing direction = accelerating, even at constant speed.

questions.question: The slope of a VELOCITY vs. time graph gives you:
questions.explanation: Slope of position vs. time = velocity. Slope of velocity vs. time = acceleration.

questions.question: A skeleton racer enters the sled at 5.3 m/s and accelerates at a constant 1 m/s/s down the track. What's the displacement 3 s later?
Ty pitches a baseball at 101 mph. The release point is 17.5 m from the plate. About how much time does the batter have?
Cumulative 10 m splits: 50 m = 5.72 s, 60 m = 6.58 s, 70 m = 7.43 s, 80 m = 8.33 s. What was the top speed over these segments?
questions.explanation: Find the time for each 10 m chunk: 0.86 s, 0.85 s, 0.90 s. Fastest chunk (60-70 m): 10 / 0.85 = 11.76 m/s. Dividing the total distance by total time only gives the average speed.

questions.question: Which change will ALWAYS increase running speed?
options: Increase stride rate while shortening stride length
Lengthen stride length while lowering stride rate
Increase both stride rate and stride length
Keep stride rate the same while shortening stride length
questions.explanation: Speed = stride length x stride rate. Raising both always raises the product. Trading one for the other can go either way.

questions.question: A rowing shell moves upstream at 8 mph relative to the water, and the river flows downstream at 1 mph. What's the shell's velocity relative to the riverbank?
questions.explanation: Opposite directions, so subtract: 8 - 1 = 7 mph upstream.

blocks.p: A **projectile** is anything that's been launched and is now coasting on its own inertia. Once it's in the air, the only forces on it are **gravity** and **air resistance**. A shot put, a basketball, a diver, a long jumper mid-flight: all projectiles. A jet plane isn't, because its engines keep pushing it.

This is the whole trick to the chapter. Gravity only pulls **vertically**, so (ignoring air resistance) nothing changes the **horizontal velocity**. It stays constant the entire flight. Meanwhile the vertical velocity drops by 9.8 m/s every second. You solve the two directions totally separately and connect them with time.

head: Horizontal
Vertical
rows: Starts at vᵧ, hits 0 at the peak, ends at -vᵧ (same height)

list: **At the instant of takeoff** (no longer touching the ground): vertical acceleration is **-9.8 m/s/s**. While still on the ground, the ground is pushing too, so it isn't -9.8 until the moment she leaves.
**At the peak:** vertical **velocity** is 0, but vertical **acceleration** is still -9.8. Gravity never takes a break.
**Throughout a shot put's flight:** vertical acceleration is a constant -9.8. It does not change on the way up vs. down.

blocks.p: Problems usually give you a resultant speed and an angle, like 13.1 m/s at 39°. Before any projectile equation, split it: `vᵧ = v sin θ` and `vₓ = v cos θ`. If they give you the components instead and want the resultant, go back with Pythagoras and inverse tangent.

Three release factors: **velocity, angle, and height**. Small changes in angle or height barely move the landing spot, but small changes in **release velocity** make a big difference, since speed increases both the flight time and the horizontal velocity. So training should focus on velocity first.

list: 45° is the best angle only when release and landing heights are equal and air resistance doesn't matter.
When release height is **above** the landing height (like a shot put), the best angle drops **below 45°**.
For a javelin, air resistance (lift and drag) matters a lot, so the best angle isn't 45° there either.

blocks.key: Once airborne: horizontal velocity constant, vertical acceleration -9.8 the whole time, even at the peak and at the instant of takeoff. Release velocity matters most for distance.

example.q: A shot put leaves the hand at 14 m/s at 42°. What are the vertical and horizontal components?
A baseball leaves with 47.0 m/s horizontal and 4.1 m/s vertical. What's the resultant velocity?

lessons.title: Flight time, max height, and distance

blocks.p: There are really just three things to calculate, and they're all on your equation sheet. The main decision is which flight time equation to grab.

head: What you want
Equation
Notes
rows: Square vᵧ first. Don't forget to add the starting height.
Flight time, same start and land height
The short one. Peak time is half of this.
The long one. Y₀ = how far above the landing it starts (positive).
Use the horizontal velocity, not the resultant.

blocks.p: Since g = -9.8, the negatives cancel out. A shortcut for max height: vᵧ² / 19.6 + Y₀. For the short flight time: 2vᵧ / 9.8.

steps: Split the release velocity: vᵧ = v sin θ, vₓ = v cos θ.
Ask: does it land at the same height it started? Yes = short flight time equation. No = long one.
Plug in vᵧ (the vertical part, not the resultant!).
Distance = vₓ x flight time.
Sanity check: max height should be a bit above the start, flight times are usually a couple seconds or less for sports, and nothing should come out negative.

blocks.tip: When the numbers come as ranges on the exam, a weird result (negative, or way outside every range) means a setup mistake. The usual culprits: forgetting to square vᵧ, forgetting to add Y₀, or using the resultant velocity instead of vᵧ.

blocks.key: Use vᵧ for height and time, vₓ for distance. Short flight time when heights match, long one when they don't. Add the starting height to max height.

example.q: Morgan's vertical velocity at takeoff is 4.4 m/s and his center of gravity is at 1.31 m. Peak height?
A shot put is released at 13.1 m/s at 39°, 1.6 m above the ground. Flight time?
A football is thrown with vᵧ = 2 m/s and vₓ = 20 m/s and caught at the same height. Flight time, landing vertical velocity, and distance?
example.a: FT = 2(2) / 9.8 = **0.41 s**. It lands with **-2 m/s** vertically (same speed, opposite direction). Distance = 20 x 0.41 = **8.2 m**.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a projectile?
questions.explanation: A projectile coasts on its own inertia with only gravity and air resistance acting. A jet has engines constantly pushing it.

questions.question: Ignoring air resistance, what happens to a projectile's HORIZONTAL velocity during its flight?
options: It decreases at 9.8 m/s every second
It stays constant the whole flight
It increases on the way down
It hits zero at the peak
questions.explanation: Gravity only acts vertically, so nothing changes horizontal velocity.

questions.question: Throughout the flight of a shot put, the vertical acceleration...
options: is positive going up, negative coming down
questions.explanation: Gravity is the only vertical force in flight, so vertical acceleration is -9.8 the whole time.

questions.question: Alice leaves the ground in the high jump with a vertical velocity of 4.0 m/s. What's her vertical acceleration at the instant of takeoff (when she's no longer touching the ground)?
questions.explanation: Once she's off the ground, gravity is the only force, so it's -9.8. Her velocity doesn't change that.

questions.question: At the very top of a basketball player's jump, which of these are true? (Select all that apply)
options: Horizontal velocity is the same as at takeoff
questions.explanation: At the peak, vertical velocity is 0 but gravity is still accelerating him at -9.8. Horizontal velocity hasn't changed since takeoff.

questions.question: A shot put is released at 12.5 m/s at an angle of 39°. What's its VERTICAL velocity component?
questions.explanation: Vertical is opposite the angle: 12.5 x sin 39° = 7.87 m/s.

questions.question: A baseball is thrown with a horizontal velocity of 47.0 m/s and a vertical velocity of 4.1 m/s. What's the resultant velocity?
questions.explanation: √(47² + 4.1²) = 47.2 m/s. Angle = tan⁻¹(4.1 / 47) = 5.0° above horizontal.

questions.question: Ignoring air resistance, a football thrown with a vertical velocity of +2 m/s comes back down to the height it was thrown. What's its vertical velocity at that moment?
questions.explanation: Same height means the same vertical speed, just pointing the other way.

questions.question: Which release factor has the biggest effect on how far a shot put travels?
questions.explanation: Small changes in velocity raise both flight time and horizontal velocity, so distance jumps. Angle and height changes have smaller effects.

questions.question: A shot put is released from well above the landing height. Compared with 45°, the optimal release angle for distance will be:
questions.explanation: 45° is only optimal when release and landing heights match. With a higher release, the best angle drops below 45°.

questions.question: Why isn't the optimal release angle 45° for the javelin?
options: Air resistance, not just gravity, changes its path
The javelin is far too heavy for a 45° release
Throwers can't physically release that high
Gravity is weaker on a long, thin object like it
questions.explanation: With a javelin, lift and drag forces are big enough to change the trajectory, so the simple 45° rule doesn't apply.

questions.question: Meghan high jumps over a bar at 2.01 m. At takeoff her vertical velocity is 4.1 m/s and her center of gravity is 1.27 m high. What peak height does her center of gravity reach?
questions.explanation: MH = vᵧ² / 19.6 + Y₀ = 16.81 / 19.6 + 1.27 = 2.13 m. Forgetting to square, forgetting Y₀, or skipping the 2 are the usual traps.

questions.question: A ball is launched with vᵧ = 10 m/s and vₓ = 5 m/s and lands at the same height. What's its flight time?
questions.explanation: Same heights, so FT = 2vᵧ / 9.8 = 20 / 9.8 = 2.04 s. 1.02 s is only the time to the peak.

questions.question: Same ball (vᵧ = 10 m/s, vₓ = 5 m/s, same landing height). How far does it travel horizontally?
questions.explanation: HD = vₓ x FT = 5 x 2.04 = 10.2 m. Use horizontal velocity, not vertical or resultant.

questions.question: Phil leaves the ground with a vertical velocity of 3.5 m/s to dunk. How long until he reaches his peak height?
questions.explanation: Peak is halfway through the flight (same heights): full flight = 2(3.5)/9.8 = 0.71 s, so the peak is at 0.36 s.

questions.question: A shot put is released at 13.1 m/s at 39°, 1.7 m above the ground, and lands on the ground. What's its flight time? (g = -9.8)
questions.explanation: vᵧ = 13.1 sin 39° = 8.24 m/s. It starts above the landing, so use the long equation: 1.87 s. The short equation (1.68 s) ignores the 1.7 m drop.

questions.question: A shot put leaves the hand at 15 m/s at 42° from a height of 1.3 m. What's its maximum height?
Chad punts a football at 18 m/s at 48°, leaving his foot 0.8 m off the ground. Where is the ball 1.5 s later?
questions.explanation: X = vₓt = 12.04 x 1.5 = 18.1 m. Y = 0.8 + 13.38(1.5) + ½(-9.8)(1.5²) = 9.8 m. Forgetting the gravity term gives way too high.

blocks.p: Kinetics is about the **causes** of motion, which means forces. Newton's three laws are the foundation, and the exam loves asking which law is which.

head: Law
Nickname
What it says in plain words
rows: Things keep doing what they're doing (sitting still or moving straight at a constant speed) unless a net external force changes it.
Acceleration is proportional to the force and in the same direction as it, and inversely proportional to mass. Twice the mass, half the acceleration for the same force.
Push on something and it pushes back on you just as hard in the opposite direction.

blocks.h: What the first law really means

blocks.p: Equilibrium (zero net force) does **not** mean no motion. It means no **change** in motion. A gliding hockey puck and a dumbbell being lifted at a steady speed both have zero net force. Gravity makes this tricky vertically, but horizontally it's easy to see: in projectile motion, horizontal velocity stays constant because there's no horizontal force.

list: Can a body move with no external forces? **Yes**, at a constant velocity.
Can it change direction with no external forces? **No**, changing direction is acceleration, which needs a net force.
Can it move at a constant velocity while external forces act? **Yes**, if they cancel out.
Pull a tug-of-war rope with 50 lb and the rope pulls back with **50 lb** (third law).

blocks.p: When you walk or run, you push **down and back** on the ground, and the ground pushes **up and forward** on you. That reaction force is what actually moves you. This is also why "external force" questions use the ground's push on the athlete, not the athlete's push on the ground.

The F in F = ma is always the **net** (resultant) force. So to lift a barbell off the floor you need **more** than its weight, because exactly its weight just cancels gravity (net force zero, no acceleration). And when the ground pushes up with exactly body weight, the body isn't accelerating at all.

Every pair of objects pulls on each other: `F = G m₁ m₂ / r²`. For two people that force is tiny. But Earth's mass is huge, and when you plug it in, the result is just your body weight, which is where g = -9.8 comes from. Different planet, different g, different weight, same mass.

blocks.key: 1st = inertia, 2nd = F = ma (acceleration proportional to force), 3rd = action-reaction. Zero net force means no acceleration, not no motion. Lifting something needs more than its weight.

example.q: A 140 lb runner's average vertical ground reaction force during stance is 1150 N. What's her average vertical acceleration?
example.a: Weight = 140 x 4.45 = 623 N, mass = 623 / 9.8 = 63.6 kg. Net vertical force = 1150 - 623 = 527 N. a = 527 / 63.6 = **8.3 m/s/s** upward.

blocks.p: **Linear momentum** is mass times velocity, `L = mv`, in kg·m/s. A big lineman jogging and a small sprinter at top speed can have similar momentum.
**Impulse** is force applied over time, `FΔt`. The impulse-momentum equation says impulse equals the **change** in momentum: `FΔt = mΔv`. It comes straight from F = ma, since a = Δv / Δt.

blocks.h: The two traps he warned about

list: **F is the average RESULTANT force.** If someone lifts a dancer with 500 N, that's not the F. Gravity is pulling her down too, so F = 500 - her weight.

**Δv is a change, so it's final minus initial.** Landing at 4 m/s downward and stopping: Δv = 0 - (-4) = +4 m/s. And if they want a final velocity, add the change to whatever velocity was there before.

blocks.p: The same change in momentum can come from a big force over a short time or a small force over a long time. A landing mat **stretches the time**, so the force on the body drops. Following through on a swing keeps the bat on the ball a little **longer**, so more momentum gets transferred.

steps: Get mass in kg (divide lb by 2.2) and velocity in m/s.
Find the net force: applied force minus weight (if it's vertical).
FΔt = mΔv, solve for the unknown.
If they want a height after a throw, take the release velocity and use max height: v² / 19.6 + starting height.

blocks.key: Momentum = mv. Impulse = FΔt = mΔv, where F is the NET force (subtract weight when it's vertical) and Δv = final - initial.

example.q: A 50 kg gymnast lands moving 4 m/s downward and stops in 0.5 s. Average resultant force?
Jenna (40 kg) is standing still. Tyrel pushes up with 500 N for 0.8 s. What's her velocity when he lets go?
example.a: Net force = 500 - (40 x 9.8) = 500 - 392 = 108 N. Δv = 108 x 0.8 / 40 = **2.16 m/s**. Using 500 N would give 10 m/s, way too fast.

example.q: Allyson Felix (125 lb) runs 23 mph. What's her momentum?

blocks.p: **Conservation of momentum:** if the net external force on a system is zero, the total momentum stays the same through a collision. It can shift from one object to the other, but the total doesn't change: `m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂` (u = before, v = after). Pick a positive direction and stick with it.

head: Collision type
What happens
e
rows: Bounce, but some energy turns to heat and sound

blocks.p: **e** measures how bouncy a collision is. It's a ratio, so it has **no units**, and it ranges from 0 to 1. Two ways to get it:

list: Drop test: `e = √(bounce height / drop height)`. Don't forget the square root!
Velocities: `e = (v₂ - v₁) / (u₁ - u₂)`, the separation speed after divided by the approach speed before.

blocks.p: Key concept: e belongs to the **pair** of objects colliding, not to one object alone. A basketball on hardwood has a different e than the same ball on grass. Things that change e: the materials, a ball's age, string tension. And per the textbook, **within a normal range of impact speeds, e stays about the same.** Drop it from a bit higher and it bounces proportionally higher.

blocks.tip: You missed the "what happens to e as impact speed increases" quiz question. The textbook says e is based on the objects' properties, not impact velocity, so through a narrow range of speeds it stays about the same. (At really extreme impacts the materials themselves change, and then e can drop.)

blocks.p: Why can a tennis ball leave the racket faster than the racket is moving? The ball has a small mass, so the momentum it gains mostly shows up as **velocity**.

blocks.key: Momentum is conserved when net external force is zero. e = √(bounce / drop) or (v₂ - v₁)/(u₁ - u₂), unitless, 0 to 1, and a property of the two objects together.

example.q: A penny (2.5 g) moving 1.1 m/s hits a resting nickel (5.0 g) and stops. How fast does the nickel go?
example.a: 2.5 x 1.1 = 5.0 x v, so v = **0.55 m/s**. Twice the mass, half the velocity. (The units cancel, so grams are fine here.)

example.q: A ball dropped from 1.00 m bounces to 0.59 m. What's e?

questions.question: Which of Newton's laws is also called the Law of Inertia?
questions.explanation: The first law: an object keeps its state of rest or constant straight-line motion unless a net force acts. That resistance is inertia.

questions.question: Which of Newton's laws says that an object's acceleration is proportional to the force impressed on it?
questions.explanation: The second law, F = ma: acceleration is proportional to the force, in its direction, and inversely proportional to mass.

questions.question: Which law is described by "action-reaction"?
questions.explanation: Third law: every force has an equal and opposite reaction force.

questions.question: You pull on a tug-of-war rope with a force of 50 lb. How much force does the rope exert on you?
questions.explanation: Third law: the rope pulls back on you with an equal and opposite force.

questions.question: Which of these situations are possible? (Select all that apply)
options: A body moving with no external forces acting on it
A body moving at constant velocity while external forces act on it
A body changing direction with no external forces acting on it
A body accelerating while the resultant force on it is zero
questions.explanation: With no forces, it can coast at constant velocity. Forces that cancel also give constant velocity. But changing direction or accelerating requires a non-zero net force.

questions.question: You're trying to lift a 50 kg barbell off the ground. What's the minimum upward force you need?
questions.explanation: Weight = 50 x 9.8 = 490 N. Exactly 490 N only balances gravity. To accelerate it upward you need a net upward force, so more than 490 N.

questions.question: During a vertical jump, the ground's upward force on the jumper equals her body weight at one instant. What's true about her acceleration at that instant?
options: She's accelerating upward at that instant
She's accelerating downward at that instant
There's no acceleration at that instant
questions.explanation: Ground force = weight means the net force is zero, so acceleration is zero (F = ma).

questions.question: If a jumper had more mass but produced the exact same forces on the ground, what would happen?
options: Accelerations and jump height would be higher
Accelerations and jump height wouldn't change
It depends entirely on body position
Accelerations and jump height would be lower
questions.explanation: Same force, more mass: smaller net force (more weight to overcome) and a = F/m gets smaller. Lower takeoff velocity, lower jump.

questions.question: During the stance phase, a 140 lb runner exerts an average vertical force of 1150 N. What's her average vertical acceleration?
The product of a body's mass and its linear velocity is called:
questions.explanation: L = mv. Impulse is force x time, and it equals the change in momentum.

questions.question: Which quantity is equal to a change in linear momentum?
questions.explanation: FΔt = mΔv. Impulse is the change in momentum.

questions.question: Frank Fredericks (161 lb) runs 27 mph in a straight line. What's his momentum?
questions.explanation: Mass = 161 / 2.2 = 73.2 kg. Speed = 27 x 1609 / 3600 = 12.07 m/s. L = 883 kg·m/s. Mass must be in kg, not lb or N.

questions.question: A 55 kg gymnast lands from a jump moving 3.2 m/s downward and comes to a stop in 0.45 s. What's the average resultant force on her during the landing?
questions.explanation: Δv = 0 - (-3.2) = 3.2 m/s. F = mΔv / Δt = 55 x 3.2 / 0.45 = 391 N. This is the resultant, so you don't add or subtract weight.

questions.question: Jenna (44 kg) is standing still when Tyrel lifts and throws her with an average vertical force of 630 N for 0.7 s. What's her vertical velocity when he releases her? (g = -9.8)
questions.explanation: Net force = 630 - (44 x 9.8) = 198.8 N. Δv = 198.8 x 0.7 / 44 = 3.16 m/s. Using the full 630 N is the trap he warned about.

questions.question: Jane (55 kg) is standing still. The RESULTANT vertical force on her is 130 N for 0.9 s during a lift. Her center of gravity is 1.4 m high when released. How high will it get?
questions.explanation: Δv = 130 x 0.9 / 55 = 2.13 m/s (130 N is already the resultant). Max height = 2.13² / 19.6 + 1.4 = 1.63 m.

questions.question: Why does a soft landing mat reduce the force on a high jumper compared with concrete?
options: It reduces the momentum the jumper has when landing
It increases the change in velocity during the landing
It lowers the jumper's mass as the mat compresses
It increases the time over which momentum is reduced
questions.explanation: Same change in momentum either way. Spreading it over more time (FΔt = mΔv) means less force.

questions.question: Total momentum of a system is conserved during a collision when:
options: The net external force on the system is zero
Both objects have the same mass
The objects move in the same direction
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum requires zero net external force on the system.

questions.question: A penny (2.5 g) moving at 1.1 m/s collides with a resting nickel (5.0 g). If the penny stops, how fast does the nickel move?
questions.explanation: Momentum before = after: 2.5 x 1.1 = 5.0 x v, so v = 0.55 m/s.

questions.question: A ball is dropped from 1.00 m and rebounds to 0.59 m. What's the coefficient of restitution?
questions.explanation: e = √(bounce / drop) = √0.59 = 0.77. Forgetting the square root gives 0.59.

questions.question: A tennis ball is dropped onto the court from 100 inches and bounces to 55 inches. What's e?
questions.explanation: √(55 / 100) = 0.74. No unit conversion needed since it's a ratio.

questions.question: Which statement about the coefficient of restitution is correct?
options: It depends on both objects and has no units
It belongs to one object and is in m/s
It can be any value greater than one
It goes up whenever the drop height rises
questions.explanation: e is a unitless ratio between 0 and 1, and it describes the collision between two specific objects.

questions.question: According to the textbook, what happens to the coefficient of restitution as impact speed increases through a relatively narrow range of speeds?
questions.explanation: e is based on the properties of the objects, not the impact velocity, so it doesn't vary with drop height in a normal range. Only extreme impacts that change the materials would change it.

questions.question: Which of these would NOT be expected to affect the coefficient of restitution between a tennis ball and racquet?
options: The tension of the racquet strings
How old and worn out the ball is
The material the racquet is made of
questions.explanation: e is about the two objects in the collision. The court isn't part of the ball-racquet impact.

questions.question: How can a tennis ball leave the racquet moving faster than the racquet itself?
options: The coefficient of restitution there is greater than one
The racquet must be moving incredibly fast at impact
Air resistance gives the ball an extra push after impact
The ball's low mass turns gained momentum into velocity
questions.explanation: Momentum transferred to a light object shows up mostly as a big velocity. e stays below 1.

blocks.p: **Mechanical work** is a force acting through a displacement: `U = Fd`, where d is the displacement **in the direction of the force**. The unit is the **Joule** (J), which is just a Newton-meter. Work is a scalar, but it can still be positive or negative.
The sign depends on the **direction of the force** compared with the **direction of motion**. Same direction = positive work. Opposite directions = negative work.

head: Situation
Force on the object
Motion
Work
Muscle action
rows: Catching a ball in a glove

blocks.p: So over a full rep of a bench press, push-up, or pull-up, you do positive work on the way up and the same amount of negative work on the way down, and the **net mechanical work is zero**. Your pecs might not agree, but that's the physics.
Work is also the **area under a force vs. displacement graph**.

A foam pit or a catcher's glove has to do a set amount of work to stop you or the ball. Since U = Fd, **increasing the displacement** during the landing lowers the force. (It's the same idea as impulse with time, just using distance instead.)

blocks.key: U = Fd in Joules. Force and motion in the same direction = positive (concentric). Opposite = negative (eccentric). A full rep up and down = zero net work.

example.q: A person bench presses a 70 kg bar up 0.5 m. How much work do they do on the bar?
example.a: The average force needed equals the bar's weight: 70 x 9.8 = 686 N. U = 686 x 0.5 = **343 J**, positive since force and motion are both up.

example.q: A glove exerts 28 N on a baseball through 0.22 m to stop it. How much work, and what sign?
example.a: 28 x 0.22 = 6.2 J in size. The glove pushes against the ball's motion, so it's **-6.2 J** (negative).

blocks.p: **Energy** is the ability to do work, also in Joules. Three kinds show up in this class:

head: Type
Equation
Comes from
rows: Deformation: k = stiffness, x = how far it stretched

blocks.p: In KE, **velocity** matters most because it's squared. Double the mass and KE doubles, but double the velocity and KE goes up **4x**. Also watch units on strain energy: kN/m to N/m (x1000) and cm to m (/100).
Work is the change in total mechanical energy: `U = ΔKE + ΔGPE + ΔSE`. That's the bridge that lets you go from energy to force: find how much energy changed, that's the work, then F = U / d.

When the only external forces are **conservative** ones (gravity, strain/elastic, electric, magnetic). The textbook's example: a basketball player in the air. On the way up, GPE rises and KE drops, but the total stays the same until the ground touches him again.

list: Diver or jumper in the air (ignoring air resistance): **conserved**.
Hang glider: **not** conserved, since air forces are doing work.
Elevator rising at a constant velocity: net force is zero, but GPE is going up, so **not** conserved. Zero net force does NOT automatically mean conserved energy.

blocks.key: KE = ½mv² (velocity squared matters most), GPE = mgh, SE = ½kx². Work = change in energy. Energy is conserved only when gravity (or other conservative forces) is the only thing acting.

example.q: A 70 kg pole vaulter runs at 8.8 m/s with his center of gravity at 1.1 m. If all of it converts to height, how high can his center of gravity get?
example.a: KE = ½(70)(8.8²) = 2710 J. GPE = 70 x 9.8 x 1.1 = 755 J. Total = 3465 J. Height = 3465 / (70 x 9.8) = **5.05 m**. Shortcut: 8.8² / 19.6 + 1.1 gives the same thing, since the mass cancels.

example.q: A volleyball player (weight -600 N) contacts the ground at 3 m/s and leaves at 4 m/s. KE at each moment?
example.a: Mass = 600 / 9.8 = 61.2 kg. At contact: ½(61.2)(3²) = **275 J**. Leaving: ½(61.2)(4²) = **490 J**. KE is never negative since v is squared.

example.q: A 0.15 kg baseball hits a glove at 40 m/s and stops over 8 cm. What's the average force?
example.a: KE = ½(0.15)(40²) = 120 J, so the glove does -120 J of work. F = U / d = 120 / 0.08 = **1500 N**.

blocks.p: **Power** is how fast work gets done: `P = U / t`, in **Watts** (J/s). Since work is force x displacement and displacement / time is velocity, you can also write `P = Fv`.

This is the difference between a linebacker who can get to the ball carrier and one who gets there first. Plenty of athletes can do the work, but being powerful means doing it in less time, which really means producing big forces quickly.

steps: Find the work. Either U = Fd, or the change in energy (like KE gained by a thrown object).
Divide by the time the force was applied.
Or, if you have average force and average velocity, P = F x v directly.

blocks.key: P = U / t = Fv, in Watts. Same work in less time = more power.

example.q: A 60 kg student jumps 60 cm and a 90 kg student jumps 45 cm, with the same push-off time. Who's more powerful?
example.a: Work = change in GPE. 60 kg: 60 x 9.8 x 0.6 = 353 J. 90 kg: 90 x 9.8 x 0.45 = 397 J. Same time, so the **90 kg student** did more work per second, so more power.

example.q: Nick releases a 2.0 kg discus at 18 m/s horizontally after applying force for 0.58 s. Average power?

questions.question: Mechanical work is calculated as:
options: Force x displacement in the direction of the force
Force x the time the force is applied
Mass x velocity of the moving object
questions.explanation: U = Fd, in Joules. Force x time is impulse, and mass x velocity is momentum.

questions.question: Phil catches a baseball in his glove. The glove exerts 28 N through a displacement of 0.22 m. What's the MAGNITUDE of the work done on the ball?
Is the work the glove does on the ball (from the last question) positive, negative, or zero?
questions.explanation: The glove pushes against the ball's direction of motion, so the work is negative. The ball loses energy.

questions.question: The difference between positive and negative work comes from the direction of motion and the:
options: Size of the force acting on the body
Point where the force is applied
Line of action of the force on it
Direction of the force acting on the body
questions.explanation: Same direction = positive, opposite = negative. Size doesn't decide the sign.

questions.question: Lowering a barbell slowly to your chest is associated with which kind of work and muscle action?
questions.explanation: Muscle force on the bar is up, the bar moves down: negative work, with the muscles lengthening (eccentric).

questions.question: What's true about the mechanical work done on the body over one full push-up (down and back up)?
options: Positive going down, negative going up, net zero
Negative going down, positive going up, net zero
Only positive work is done the whole time
Only negative work is done the whole time
questions.explanation: Down: force up, motion down = negative. Up: both up = positive. They cancel over the full rep.

questions.question: A person bench presses a 92 kg bar from the chest up to full arm extension, 0.45 m. How much work is done on the bar?
questions.explanation: Force = bar weight = 92 x 9.8 = 902 N. U = 902 x 0.45 = 406 J, positive since force and motion are both up.

questions.question: A soft foam pit cushions a pole vaulter's landing by:
questions.explanation: Same work is needed to stop the vaulter. More displacement means less force (U = Fd).

questions.question: In the kinetic energy equation, which variable changes KE the most if you change it?
questions.explanation: KE = ½mv². Velocity is squared, so doubling it quadruples KE.

questions.question: What's the gravitational potential energy of a 79 kg slackline walker 1.3 m above the ground?
A volleyball player (weight = -600 N) lands from a spike and jumps again. She contacts the ground at 3 m/s and leaves at 4 m/s. What's her KE as she leaves the ground?
questions.explanation: Mass = 600 / 9.8 = 61.2 kg. KE = ½(61.2)(4²) = 490 J. KE can't be negative, and you need mass (not weight) in the equation.

questions.question: A volleyball is bumped straight up to 10 m above the player's arms. What was its initial velocity leaving the arms? (g = -9.8)
questions.explanation: All the KE at release becomes GPE at the top: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2 x 9.8 x 10) = 14.0 m/s. Mass cancels out.

questions.question: A 131 lb gymnast in a giant swing is 4.8 m above the ground moving 4.2 m/s. His body is stretched 15 cm with a stiffness of 34 kN/m. What's his total mechanical energy?
questions.explanation: Mass = 59.5 kg. GPE = 2801 J, KE = 525 J, SE = ½(34000)(0.15²) = 382 J. Total = 3709 J. Convert kN/m to N/m and cm to m.

questions.question: A 70 kg pole vaulter reaches 8.8 m/s at the end of his approach with his center of gravity 1.1 m high. If all his KE and GPE become GPE, how high can his center of gravity get?
questions.explanation: Total energy / (mg) = height: 8.8² / 19.6 + 1.1 = 5.05 m. Leaving out the starting 1.1 m is the common slip.

questions.question: A 0.15 kg baseball hits a catcher's glove at 40 m/s and stops over a displacement of 8 cm. What's the average force from the glove?
questions.explanation: KE = ½(0.15)(40²) = 120 J, so the glove does -120 J of work. F = U / d = 120 / 0.08 = 1500 N. Remember 8 cm = 0.08 m.

questions.question: In which of these is total mechanical energy conserved? (Ignore air resistance unless it's the main force.) (Select all that apply)
options: A diver in the air after leaving the board
An elevator rising at a constant velocity
A ball rolling to a stop on grass
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved when gravity is the only force acting: the diver and the shot put. The glider has air forces doing work, the elevator gains GPE from its cable, and grass friction drains the ball's KE.

questions.question: Mechanical power is best described as:
options: The total work done, P = F x d
The change in momentum, P = F x t
Stored energy from height, P = mgh
The rate of doing work, P = U / t
questions.explanation: Power = work / time = force x velocity, in Watts.

questions.question: In a vertical jump test, a 60 kg student jumps 60 cm and a 90 kg student jumps 45 cm. Both apply force for the same time. Who's more powerful?
questions.explanation: Work = mgh: 60 kg does 353 J, 90 kg does 397 J. Same time, so the 90 kg student has more power.

questions.question: Nick gives a 2.0 kg discus a horizontal release velocity of 18 m/s, applying force for 0.58 s. What's the average horizontal power?
Someone does a standing vertical jump from a squat. An average vertical force of 350 N is applied for 0.4 s through a displacement of 0.6 m. What's the average power during the push-off?
An athlete's mass is measured on Earth and again on the Moon, where gravity is weaker. Which is true?
options: Mass stays the same and weight is smaller on the Moon
Mass and weight both get smaller on the Moon
Mass gets smaller and weight stays the same
Mass and weight both stay exactly the same
questions.explanation: Mass is inertia and never changes with location. Weight = mg, so weaker gravity means less weight.

questions.question: A volleyball player's shoe is sliding sideways across the court as she reaches for a dig. What kind of friction acts between the shoe and the floor?
questions.explanation: Surfaces sliding relative to each other = dynamic friction. Static is for surfaces that aren't moving relative to each other.

questions.question: A sprinter coming out of the blocks pushes back (horizontally) against the block with 640 N and down (vertically) with 820 N. What's the magnitude of the resultant force?
Same sprinter (640 N back, 820 N down). What's the direction of the resultant force relative to the ground?
questions.explanation: Relative to the ground means horizontal = 0°. tan⁻¹(820 / 640) = 52.0°.

questions.question: A 58 kg ice skater is gliding across the ice. The coefficient of dynamic friction is 0.09. Ignoring air resistance, what's the frictional force on the skater?
questions.explanation: Normal force = 58 x 9.8 = 568 N. Friction = 0.09 x 568 = 51.2 N.

questions.question: The ground reaction force on a long jumper is 5600 N acting forward and upward at 72° from horizontal. What's the VERTICAL component?

A 72 kg runner exerts 210 N of horizontal force as he contacts the ground. The vertical ground reaction force is 1420 N, and 90 N of air resistance works against his motion. What's the direction of the resultant EXTERNAL force relative to the ground?
questions.explanation: Horizontal: ground pushes back 210 + air 90 = 300 N backward. Vertical: 1420 - 705.6 (weight) = 714.4 N up. tan⁻¹(714.4 / 300) = 67.2°.

questions.question: A 72 kg skier glides down a 22° slope. There's a frictional force of 95 N and air resistance of 75 N. What's the skier's acceleration down the slope?

A cheerleader does a handstand on another cheerleader's hands. The lower cheerleader weighs 180 lb and the vertical ground reaction force is 1420 N. What must the top cheerleader's mass be for equilibrium?
A diver leaves the platform and does a forward somersault on the way down to the water. What type of motion is the diver's body doing?
questions.explanation: The body travels along a curved path AND rotates, a combination of translation and rotation: general motion.

questions.question: A runner rounds the curve of a track at a perfectly constant speed. Which is true?
options: She's accelerating, because her direction keeps changing
She isn't accelerating, because her speed doesn't change
She's accelerating only if her speed also increases
She isn't accelerating, since curves don't count here
questions.explanation: Acceleration is a change in velocity, and velocity includes direction. Constant speed on a curve is still acceleration (toward the center).

questions.question: A receiver runs 48 yd along a curved path before he's tackled. The straight line from start to tackle is 35 yd at 28° to the sideline. What were his distance, resultant displacement, and yards gained?
options: Distance: 35 yd, displacement: 48 yd, yards gained: 31 yd
Distance: 48 yd, displacement: 31 yd, yards gained: 35 yd
Distance: 35 yd, displacement: 48 yd, yards gained: 35 yd
Distance: 48 yd, displacement: 35 yd, yards gained: 31 yd
questions.explanation: Distance = actual path (48). Displacement = straight line (35). Yards gained = 35 x cos 28° = 30.9 yd.

questions.question: A soccer player accelerates from 2.1 m/s to 8.9 m/s in 2.6 s. What's her acceleration?
questions.explanation: a = (final - initial) / time = (8.9 - 2.1) / 2.6 = 2.62 m/s/s.

questions.question: A pinewood derby car starts from rest down a constant slope with a constant acceleration of 2.8 m/s/s. What's its displacement after 1.5 s?
The slope of a POSITION vs. time graph gives:
questions.explanation: Position-time slope = velocity. Velocity-time slope = acceleration.

questions.question: A pitcher throws a fastball at 94 mph. The release point is 18.4 m from home plate. How much time does the batter have from release to contact?
A long jumper reaches the highest point of her flight. What's her vertical acceleration at that moment?
options: It depends on her body position
questions.explanation: Vertical velocity is zero at the peak, but gravity is still the only force, so vertical acceleration is -9.8 throughout flight.

questions.question: A high jumper's vertical velocity at takeoff (no longer touching the ground) is 4.5 m/s, and her center of gravity is 1.25 m high. What peak height does her center of gravity reach?
options: Less than 2.15 m above the ground
Between 2.15 and 2.25 m above the ground
Between 2.25 and 2.35 m above the ground
More than 2.35 m above the ground

questions.question: A shot put is released at 13.6 m/s at an angle of 38°, 1.8 m above the ground, and lands on the ground. What's its flight time? Ignore air resistance and use g = -9.8 m/s/s.
questions.explanation: vᵧ = 13.6 sin 38° = 8.37 m/s. Heights differ, so use the long equation: (-8.37 - √(8.37² - 2(-9.8)(1.8))) / -9.8 = 1.90 s.

questions.question: Same shot put (13.6 m/s at 38°, released at 1.8 m). How far does it travel horizontally before landing?
A soccer ball is kicked with a vertical velocity of 6 m/s and a horizontal velocity of 15 m/s, and lands at the same height it was kicked from. How far does it travel horizontally?
A shot putter releases the shot well above ground level. Ignoring air resistance, the release angle that gives the greatest horizontal distance would be:
questions.explanation: 45° is optimal only when release and landing heights are equal. A higher release lowers the optimal angle.

questions.question: When a sprinter pushes down and back on the ground, the ground pushes up and forward on the sprinter. Which law of motion describes this?
questions.explanation: Action-reaction is the third law.

questions.question: A runner (weight = 150 lb) runs 21 mph in a straight line. What is his momentum?
A 48 kg gymnast lands from a jump moving 3.6 m/s downward and comes to a stop in 0.40 s. What's the average resultant force on her during the landing?

A dancer (42 kg) is standing still when her partner lifts and throws her, exerting an average vertical force of 560 N for 0.75 s. What's her vertical velocity when he releases her? Use g = -9.8 m/s/s.
A ball is dropped from 1.50 m and rebounds to a height of 0.92 m. What's the coefficient of restitution?
A penny (2.5 g) moving at 1.6 m/s collides with a resting nickel (5.0 g). If the penny comes to a stop, how fast will the nickel be moving?
A coach drops the same basketball onto the same gym floor from 1 m and then from 2 m. What would you expect for the coefficient of restitution?
questions.explanation: e depends on the properties of the ball and floor, not on drop height. The ball just bounces proportionally higher.

questions.question: A person lowers an 80 kg barbell under control from full arm extension to the chest, a displacement of 0.4 m. How much work does the person do on the bar?
questions.explanation: Force on the bar = its weight, 784 N, pointing up. Displacement is -0.4 m (down). U = 784 x -0.4 = -314 J. Negative work, eccentric action.

questions.question: As a basketball player lands from a rebound, his quadriceps lengthen while controlling the knee bend. What kind of work are the quads doing?
options: No work, since nothing is lifted
questions.explanation: Muscle force opposes the direction of motion while the muscle lengthens: negative work, eccentric action.

questions.question: A 75 kg pole vaulter reaches 9.1 m/s at the end of his approach, with his center of gravity 1.05 m high. If all his kinetic and gravitational energy becomes gravitational energy, about how high can his center of gravity get?
questions.explanation: KE + GPE = GPE at the top. Mass cancels: h = 9.1² / 19.6 + 1.05 = 4.22 + 1.05 = 5.27 m.

questions.question: An athlete throws a 3.0 kg medicine ball, accelerating it from rest to 9 m/s while applying force for 0.45 s. What's the average power applied to the ball?
In which situation is total mechanical energy conserved?
options: A gymnast in the air during a dismount
A cyclist coasting to a stop on a flat road
An elevator rising at a constant speed
A paraglider drifting down to the ground
questions.explanation: In the air (ignoring air resistance), gravity is the only force, so energy just shifts between KE and GPE. The others all have non-conservative forces doing work.
